title: The Fog of Tech
gist: Mara Karlin warns of a 'technology trap': confidence in how AI, drones and other new tech will change war obscures war's unchanging fundamentals (ends, ways, coalitions, human cost), as seen in Ukraine, the 2026 US-Israeli war on Iran and past conflicts, and risks miscalculation and hollowed deterrence.

insights.claim: Policymakers across the spectrum assume technology will determine future warfare, but excessive certainty about how technology changes war while neglecting its unchanging fundamentals is dangerous.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Defense-tech narratives are prone to overconfidence; be wary of procurement thesis priced on certain battlefield outcomes.
insights.quote: in which policymakers develop a misplaced sense of certainty about how innovations will change war

insights.claim: Today's key technologies have low barriers to entry (cheap to produce, knowledge democratized), so adversaries face more equal battlefields and advantages may be short-lived; in Ukraine, fishermen's nets are one of the most effective antidrone defenses.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Cheap, mass-produced systems and low-tech countermeasures can erode expensive high-end platforms' advantage.
insights.locator: Predicting the role of technology in future wars

insights.claim: The 2018 National Defense Strategy, drafted under Elbridge Colby, predicted a few high-end capabilities (AI, robotics, hypersonics, biotechnology) would ensure victory, and a senior Pentagon official called the F-35 'a war winner' in 2017; instead Ukraine looks like 'World War I meets World War III'.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Exquisite-platform forecasts failed; value mass, cheap and attritable systems.
insights.locator: Focusing too much on procuring the shiniest equipment

insights.claim: Cheap Iranian drones have attacked soft targets in Gulf Arab states since February during the US-Israeli war on Iran, an outcome few would have predicted a dozen years ago.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.locator: A sense of certainty that sophisticated tech would dominate

themes.theme: Technology and the decision to go to war

insights.claim: Leaders often mistakenly believe technology lowers the political cost of war, especially by reducing casualties; this likely influenced Russia's 2022 invasion, as Shoigu claimed over 70 percent of the military had advanced weapons, which conferred little advantage within weeks.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Overconfidence from technological reform has produced miscalculated wars.
insights.locator: Perhaps the most perilous time for leaders

insights.claim: The 2026 US-Israeli attempt to topple Iran's regime was shaped by belief in American military sophistication, but the regime withstood the onslaught and managed to close the Strait of Hormuz, exposing the limits of the capabilities Hegseth called 'nearly unlimited'.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: The Iran war's outcomes challenge assumptions of US military dominance and carry energy-transit risk.
insights.locator: The same goes for the U.S.-Israeli attempt

insights.claim: The Trump administration launched the 2026 Iran war without a clearly articulated goal, hoping technological wizardry would achieve a long wish list without prioritizing or confronting tradeoffs.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Unclear end state raises the odds of a prolonged conflict.
insights.locator: Before launching the 2026 war on Iran

insights.claim: Ways to avoid the trap include defining a theory of victory and Clausewitzian center of gravity before war, and conducting regular impartial reviews of lessons learned; Iran studied the 2025 strikes and devolved command and control, helping the regime survive.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Adaptive adversaries learn quickly from strikes; decentralized command improves regime survivability.
insights.locator: There are ways to avoid the technology trap

insights.claim: The US and Israel launched the 2026 Iran war relying solely on each other; several allies initially denied access to territory, bases and airspace, disrupting a US way of war that depends on a global basing network.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Basing access is a real constraint on US power projection.
insights.locator: In early 2026, the United States and Israel launched the war

insights.claim: Arab Gulf states Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have used force against Iran at times without joining the coalition, but it did not influence the battlefield, while Iran used Hezbollah's cheap drones and rockets and Russia helped Iran target US facilities in the Gulf.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Gulf security is entangled with Iranian proxy and Russian support networks.
insights.locator: As the war has dragged on

insights.claim: European defense planners face a trilemma: integrating a modernized Ukrainian military, managing Germany's military buildup, and hedging against possible US aggression after Trump mused about Greenland; prioritizing one makes the other two harder and no technology resolves it.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Supports sustained but internally contested European defense spending.

insights.claim: It is unclear that AI targeting and autonomous systems have improved civilian protection: in Gaza the Israeli military approved targets from the Lavender AI system rapidly, and AI reflects rules of engagement that were loosened after October 7.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Regulatory and reputational risk around AI-enabled targeting.

insights.claim: An experiment with around 2,000 Israeli military personnel found 'algorithmic aversion' in high-collateral-damage scenarios, a desire to rely on human decision-making.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Humans may resist machine recommendations in the most consequential decisions.

insights.claim: Technology that makes military targets harder to attack can raise civilian vulnerability by increasing collateral damage risk and giving parties incentive to attack soft targets.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Infrastructure and civilian targets face higher risk.
insights.locator: Ironically, civilians may become more vulnerable

insights.claim: Low-casualty precedents repeatedly mislead: only 143 of nearly 700,000 US personnel died in the 1990-91 Gulf War, yet Mogadishu cost 18 deaths in a fight with low-tech militants and Afghanistan and Iraq became grinding; the January Venezuela operation to capture Maduro used over 150 aircraft and drones plus special forces, space and cyber platforms.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Technology reduces US risk in short raids but not in prolonged conflicts against adversaries who see war as existential.
insights.locator: This desire for immaculate war is not new

insights.claim: Replacing personnel with machines could shrink militaries, widening the gap between the public and those who serve, and eroding the principle that war-making reflects popular will.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Weaker civil-military ties could ease political resort to force.

insights.claim: Countries that have not fought in decades, such as China, may be more susceptible to the technology trap, and overconfidence on both sides could hollow out deterrence and create an escalation spiral over demonstrating will.
insights.speaker: Mara Karlin
insights.so_what: Raises miscalculation risk in US-China tensions, including over Taiwan.
insights.locator: Countries that haven't waged war in many decades
